headline: Four Pacific Nations Unite to Create Massive Ocean Sanctuary
meta_description: Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Solomon Islands are building the Melanesian Ocean Corridor of Reserves to protect one of Earth's richest marine ecosystems.
summary_short: Four Melanesian countries are linking marine reserves across the Coral Triangle, home to three-quarters of known coral species and countless endangered animals.
body:
Four Pacific island nations are building an ambitious network of connected marine reserves across some of the world's most biodiverse ocean waters. Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Solomon Islands announced the Melanesian Ocean Corridor of Reserves—Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu in May, with Solomon Islands joining in June. The corridor will link protected areas across national waters and eventually may extend into the high seas, creating a unified system to safeguard one of Earth's most remarkable ecosystems.

The Melanesian region sits within the Coral Triangle in the southwestern Pacific, which holds an estimated three-quarters of all known coral species. These waters teem with sharks, rays, dugongs, whales, and countless species still being discovered by scientists. By connecting individual reserves—including Papua New Guinea's planned 214,000-square-kilometer no-take sanctuary in western Manus and Vanuatu's 71,000-square-kilometer fully protected area around Torba Province—the corridor could safeguard migration routes, spawning grounds, and the movement of larvae between reefs. Linking these zones also makes it harder for industrial fishing vessels to exploit boundaries between reserves.

The plan remains in early stages. Maps, governance structures, enforcement systems, and funding remain undetermined. A critical question is how Indigenous communities, who have managed fishing grounds through customary tenure for generations, will participate in governing the corridor. The Pacific Regional Environment Programme is developing the legal framework, but establishing boundaries, securing resources, and creating credible enforcement will take time. Until these pieces fall into place, the corridor represents a powerful declaration of intent—proof that island nations are willing to act boldly to protect their marine heritage for future generations.
quick_facts: Papua New Guinea planning 214,000 sq km no-take sanctuary in western Manus
Coral Triangle contains three-quarters of Earth's known coral species
Four nations: Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu, Fiji, Solomon Islands
Vanuatu protecting 71,000 sq km around Torba Province
